articles.content:
"Hunting Alice Bell" is a new thriller about the dangers of online sleuthing from an unusual source.

Co-created by comedian David Baddiel and The Guardian's long-time TV critic Peter Bradshaw, it tells the story of five women who find themselves the target of some of the internet's most toxic impulses after they are each accused of being an accomplice to a notorious murderer. The six-episode show opens with Fran, played by Alexandra Roach ("Lazarus"), an ordinary working mother whose life is turned upside down when she finds her name and face plastered all over social media alongside claims she enabled killer surgeon Jason Nash (Simon Pegg). But Fran soon realizes she's not the only innocent woman who's been implicated. "Basically the women band together and they come out fighting as a unit,” Baddiel tells Variety . “And that creates its own reaction because often the internet is reaction and then more reaction to the reaction.” blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

The show, which premiered last week on Channel 4 in the U.K. (Sphere Abacus are repping global sales) was inspired, in part, by a documentary about Maxine Carr, a British teaching assistant who in 2002 notoriously provided an alibi for her boyfriend, Ian Huntley, before he was convicted of abducting and murdering two young schoolgirls.

The case caused uproar at the time and after serving a brief jail sentence she was given a court-ordered new identity and has lived in anonymity since her release (Huntley, who was given a life sentence, died earlier this year after being attacked in prison). Even so, stories about Carr have become a tabloid staple in the U.K., often peppered with tantalizing details about her new life. ("Incredibly, even now, in the last few years, you see in the Mail and the Sun stories about ‘Maxine Carr has been spotted,'" says Bradshaw.) blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Baddiel and Bradshaw originally wrote "Hunting Alice Bell" as a film before adapting it into a series for Clapperboard and Channel 4 alongside writers Polly Buckle and Kate Verghese. "We got quite close, but it never quite got made as a film," Baddiel says. "I gave up on it for a little while. And then we had the idea of ‘let's invite social media into the room.'"

The social media element – which didn't exist when Carr was convicted – has echoes of other recent British stories that have ignited the internet in recent years, from Lucy Letby, a nurse convicted in 2023 of murdering seven babies, whose innocence has been endlessly dissected online, to Nicola Bulley, whose disappearance that same year caused the U.K. media and livestreaming looky-loos to descend on her small village , with some even accusing her husband of murder (Bulley died after accidentally falling into a river; her body was found by a tarot reader a few weeks later).

On the other side of the pond, Lindsay Clancy's recent trial attracted a similar amount of morbid fascination and online sleuthing , with obsessives claiming it was Clancy's husband who murdered the couple's three children.

"I think there is [an element of public shaming] in this, yes, because it's about ordinary women who suddenly wake up and they're the center of toxic attention,” Baddiel warns. “And that can happen to anyone."

Read on for more about how Baddiel produced the show and whether it could return for a second season.

It is a departure for me. I have a thing which is — every time I say it, it sounds pretentious, but it is just true — primarily I am a storyteller… And for me, if I'm good at storytelling, then I can tell a children's book or I can tell a funny story, or I can tell a thriller.

It's an unusual thriller and it does include elements of comedy in it, which is very deliberate… in real life, people make jokes in terrible situations and we just wanted to reflect that, and also just to give it a texture that was different…So it is a departure, but at heart, in terms of what I do, it doesn't feel that much like one.

I was working on a completely different idea for Clapperboard and ITV, not a drama idea. And they just said to me, “Do you have any thrillers?” And I said, “Well, I've got this kind of weird idea for a thriller, are you interested?” And they were. And they're really good at getting stuff made. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

I was entirely hands on. I showran it. I was on set every day. At one point I was living in a shed. I think I was told not to mention this because people don't want to talk about it being kind of unglamorous but basically we didn't have enough money to have me and Paul [Walker, the director] in separate places, so we shared a place. He's so fantastic. But then his family came to stay for three weeks and I lived in a shed in someone's garden for that time. Quite a nice shed. Anyway, so it wasn't that glamorous.

What you have at the moment is a massive television landscape, much greater than when I was growing up or even 10 or 15 years ago. There's too much content to some extent, and so I think another problem is making sure that what gets made is good and not just IP. The thing that I have most noticed about telling people, especially other writers, about this is that they instantly say, “So what's the book? Was it a film before?" or whatever. No, no. It's an original idea. It was inspired by a documentary, but that doesn't make it IP. It's a very rare thing now, and to some extent the low cost of it is why that happens, because I don't think people are prepared to risk.

I knew that one way in which Clapperboard are able to make stuff is that they make stuff for a low tariff for drama. And that meant that we were constantly having to cut the cloth of the story to what was actually available. And at times, that also meant recutting it on set. There's a scene in I think Episode 3 meant to be outdoors. It's raining. We have no rain cover. We have no ability to shoot that somehow outside. So I just rewrite the scene on the spot to find a way of shooting it indoors. And that happens all the time.

So originally the scene at the end [of Episode 1] with Fran running away from [Amanda Abbington's] car — that was a car chase originally. Then we couldn't have a car chase and so I came up with the idea of her wanting to walk home… and then Julie's car slowly following her. I think that scene is better than it would have been as a car chase. And it's more unusual and probably a car chase within our means would have been shit anyway. But that really fits for me the small town feel of the show and sort of weirdness of it. In general, the low-budget element of it really suits this story and shows you can make good drama, hopefully, for small amounts of money. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid3' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

You have to have enormous health and safety insurance for any kind of moving interior car filming. It's not so bad with filming a car just driving. You also generally have to pay to have the street completely cut off — a country lane not so much — and you have to have numerous things in place, particularly if there's dialogue and someone's acting while they're doing it. If they're just driving it's slightly less. It's basically a nightmare.

I have an idea for a Season 2. It very much ends, this story, but there is a way in which you could have a Season 2. I would rather write something completely new, to be honest. I think it works really, really well as a limited series. But hey, I'm never saying never.

I think there is no answer. Unfortunately, I am by nature a depressive, which is why I'm a comedian, because I think that is the only answer. I can't see how things will get better because [the internet] is a massive, massive distraction for people. People want to be distracted. They also want, as Ralf [Little, who plays Graham Hunter] was saying, to have a purpose in their life.

We used to have things that were also not real but that gave us purpose, notably religion, and now we don't really have that. So what's giving us purpose? What's giving our lives meaning, what's making us feel like we matter? It's mainly the internet. Mainly like, "Oh, I'm on this thing and I've got 5000 likes. And also, people think I'm a hero because I'm attacking this person who we all hate" and all that stuff. And by the way, I think being too puritanical about it is wrong too. The internet's got loads of funny things on it. Got loads of cat pictures, which is great, and there have undeniably been marginalized voices that have risen through the internet in ways that the culture before it was ignoring. All of that is really important. Unfortunately, it coexists with just the most intense toxicity.

articles.title: ‘BerleeN_’ Director Ahmad Abdalla on Telling the ‘Extremely Surreal’ Stories of Arab Migrants Living in Berlin and ‘How We Deal With Fear’
articles.summary: For Egyptian filmmaker Ahmad Abdalla, the idea for “BerleeN_” grew out of stories shared by friends and relatives who had left their homes across the Arab world to build new lives in the German capital. During his visits to Berlin, their experiences, which he describes as often stranger than fiction, offered the basis for a […]
articles.content:
For Egyptian filmmaker Ahmad Abdalla , the idea for "BerleeN_" grew out of stories shared by friends and relatives who had left their homes across the Arab world to build new lives in the German capital. During his visits to Berlin, their experiences, which he describes as often stranger than fiction, offered the basis for a film about memory, belonging and starting over in a new city.

"With every visit, I keep hearing stories, and for me, the stories were extremely surreal," Abdalla tells Variety following the film's world premiere at the Cairo Film Festival . blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Peter Alsted’s Animal Conservation Doc ‘Dr. Hedgehog’ Boarded by Autlook Filmsales Ahead of IDFA Forum (EXCLUSIVE) Amanda Seyfried to Make Her Debut as 'Saturday Night Live' Host

Rather than build the film around a single protagonist, Abdalla drew on these encounters to weave together three stories that unfold over one day in Berlin, blending drama, crime and mystery. The characters' experiences are shaped as much by the lives they left behind as by the city in which they're building new ones. "Those people behave this way because they are in Berlin," he explains.

"BerleeN_" marks Abdalla's return to Cairo Film Festival, where his previous feature, " 19B ," premiered in the International Competition in 2022. The filmmaker's credits also include "Microphone" (2010), " Rags and Tatters " (2013) and " EXT/Night " (2018).

As Abdalla developed the screenplay, he realized that beneath the characters' different circumstances lay a common thread: fear.

"The main thing I terribly wanted to speak about was fear," he explains. "How we deal with fear, and how we deal with our existence on a philosophical level." He points to the rapid changes shaping the world around us as a major source of that emotion. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

His approach was partly informed by his reading of 1970s writings on Afro-surrealism, whose reflections on the surreal nature of the Black American experience resonated with what he had observed among Arab migrants in Europe.

The film also explores how memories of home shape the experience of living somewhere new. "There's something magical about mixing your memories, your relationship with the past, and with the very existing moment," Abdalla reflects. "When you are living in Berlin right now, and you are very heavily loaded with your personal stories, with what happened to you in Cairo, what happened to you in Iraq, what happened to you in Aleppo, but you're living in this new reality."

For Abdalla, there is something inherently cinematic about capturing the moment when those different realities meet.

For lead producer Kesmat El Sayed, whose Berlin-based Seera Films produced the feature alongside veteran Egyptian producer Mohamed Hefzy's Giza-based Film Clinic, the project coincided with her own move to the German capital. A longtime admirer of Abdalla's work, she had been working primarily in documentary and "BerleeN_" became her first foray into fiction features.

The experience also introduced her to a different way of working. "You have a certain time that you have to do this in, as well as a certain budget. So the pressure is immense," she explains, contrasting the experience with documentary filmmaking, where productions can take much longer.

Making the film also deepened El Sayed's own connection to Berlin, a city she was still getting to know. "It just brought me so deeply into the city in a very fast way, in a very intense way," she recalls.

El Sayed and Abdalla also sought to involve as many Arab film professionals based in Berlin as possible, creating opportunities for artists who often struggle to find work. "We wanted to have the same representation behind the camera as we did in front of it," she emphasizes. That shared sense of ownership proved invaluable when unexpected logistical issues arose, with crew members working together to quickly find solutions.

For Hefzy, who has worked with Abdalla since 2008, the director's attention to the relationship between people and their surroundings has long distinguished his filmmaking. "Even what might seem like random shots of streets or people adds another layer to the film," Hefzy observes. "None of that is random." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Abdalla's collaborative working style extends to his actors. "I don't believe in writing a stiff script," he says. Instead, he seeks out performers "willing to play and willing to change things for the film," including improvising and contributing their own dialogue. His method was inspired in part by British filmmaker Mike Leigh.

The veteran director's approach to shooting also helps keep production costs down. "He shoots in a way that makes it not expensive. His films tend to stay under one million [dollars] and, sometimes, well under," Hefzy notes.

He estimates the budget for "BerleeN_" at around $600,000–$650,000, relatively modest for an international production. But financing independent cinema in Egypt remains difficult, Hefzy says, citing the lack of a national film fund, limited regional funding opportunities and intense competition for grants. Filmmakers frequently rely on European co-productions or pool their own resources to get projects made.

"Ahmed Abdalla's films are not made with money, they're made with love," Hefzy recalls telling the audience at the film's Cairo festival premiere.

But he believes independent filmmakers need more than resourcefulness to sustain their work. "I wish we had a clearer path to financing independent films," Hefzy says, adding that even completed projects can struggle to secure distribution.

"BerleeN_" has already sold its worldwide streaming rights to Shahid, the streaming platform owned by Saudi media conglomerate MBC Group, and is slated for an Egyptian theatrical release in early December.

The producers are pursuing further festival appearances without a sales agent, but Hefzy is cautious about the film's prospects for theatrical distribution outside the Arab world. He argues that even films selected for the world's most prestigious festivals are not guaranteed international distribution. "It's very competitive and very, very difficult for Arab films to reach global audiences," he says.

For Abdalla, the film's reception in Cairo has reinforced his willingness to embrace uncertainty. He describes audiences responding to his work in wildly different ways, a pattern dating back to his earliest features. "With this kind of cinema, you can only gamble," he says. "There's no consensus. And you can only gamble on [a film] if the story was honest enough and true enough to resonate with people." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid3' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

While he is not quite ready to move on from "BerleeN_," Abdalla is considering several stories set in Toronto. The filmmaker, who regularly spends time in the Canadian city, says his only condition for future projects set outside Egypt is a personal connection to the place. "I cannot make a film about something I don't know."

articles.title: 10 Years Ago, Amy Adams Delivered One of the Best Performances in Modern Sci-fi (And the Oscars Snubbed Her)
articles.summary: From the early 2000s on through to today, Amy Adams has shined brightly on the silver screen. Whether she is playing someone wholesome and well-intentioned or a darker character with a more sinister agenda, Adams has proven she can do it all. Thanks to her range, Adams has long been recognized as one of the […]
articles.content:
But much to the delight of genre fans, one of Adams’ most acclaimed performances actually comes from a science fiction film that was released in 2016. The film and its director have since gone on to solidify the prevalence of modern science fiction and fantasy. Still, there’s a lot to be said for the enduring power of Adams’ performance, which anchors the movie’s emotionally driven story. It’s the reason why fans are still talking about it. So why didn’t Adams — one of the most chronically Oscar-nominated (but not Oscar-winning) stars of the past 20 years — fail to get a nod for what many consider her best work?

By the mid-2010s, Adams was arguably at the peak of her powers. Following a decade of Oscar-nominated critical darlings and mainstream hits alike, she chose to star in Arrival , a science fiction drama from a rising director named Denis Villeneuve . He had earned acclaim for intense thrillers like Prisoners and Sicario , but Arrival was his first foray helming a major Hollywood genre picture. Based on the 1998 novella “Story of Your Life” by Ted Chiang, the film follows Louise Banks (Adams), a linguist brought in by the United States military to communicate with a newly landed extraterrestrial species. Meanwhile, Jeremy Renner, Forest Whitaker, and Michael Stuhlbarg turn in solid supporting turns.

Arrival earned strong reviews and brought in more than $200 million worldwide on a reported production budget of just $47 million. Since then, the film’s reputation has only grown, with fans and critics alike praising it as one of the best films of that year and among the finest sci-fi movies in recent years. Notably, Villeneuve’s momentum has just kept on going. He followed Arrival with Blade Runner 2049 and a trilogy of Dune films, which concludes this year with Dune: Part Three . But despite its eight Academy Award nominations, Arrival ’s only win was for Best Sound Editing. As a result, many fans consider the film one of the most underrated of its time.

Arrival felt like more than a stepping stone for Adams, whose career had been steadily building. If anything, it felt like a culmination. Some assumed this was her inevitable Best Actress win, following nearly 20 years on the big screen and five previous Oscar nominations. Alas, Adams wasn’t even nominated, which feels like a disservice to her contribution to the film. Granted, Arrival tells a compelling, heart-wrenching story of human nature, grief and loss, and the importance of open-minded communication. But it’s Adams’ performance that unites those themes. Without her bringing the entire piece together, the movie — and its gut-punch of a narrative twist — falls apart.

Since 2016, Adams has continued to deliver strong work in films like Nocturnal Animals and TV series like Sharp Objects and Cape Fear , but nothing has quite measured up to what she did in Arrival . She earned a sixth Oscar nomination for 2018’s Vice but hasn’t been nominated since then. Perhaps the Academy Awards assumed Adams would perhaps top herself yet again in the future. Maybe its bias against science fiction — a genre that has rarely, if ever, been given its due during awards season — held the Academy back from going all in on Adams’ performance. Or perhaps the competition was just that steep that year. In any case, Arrival still stands as the definitive Adams performance and deserves celebration on its tenth anniversary.

What are your thoughts on Arrival ? What is your favorite Amy Adams performance? Let us know in the comments!

Nicola Coughlan will not be tuning into HBO ‘s new “ Harry Potter ” series over her disagreement with J.K. Rowling ‘s views on trans rights.

In a new interview with The Observer , the “Bridgerton” star doubled down on her previous comments that she “wouldn't touch” the show “with a 10-foot pole,” despite having loved Rowling's books as a child.

"I will not be watching the new ‘Harry Potter' show and I would never be in it,” she said. “Look, I know people that are involved in those shows, and they're nice people and whatever, but it's not for me." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Phoebe Bridgers' Skeletal Transformation on 'SNL' Wasn't Just a Startling Special Effect — It Emotionally Elevated One of the Best Pop Songs Ever Written About Death Ben Affleck Raved About Robert Pattinson’s ‘The Odyssey’ Performance, Recalls Matt Damon: He Said ‘It Was Like Watching a Guy Run Into an Avalanche’

Coughlan clashed with Rowling last year after the author celebrated the U.K. Supreme Court's ruling that the legal definition of a woman is based on biological sex. Following the decision, Rowling posted a photo of herself on X smoking a cigar with the caption: “I love it when a plan comes together.”

In response, Coughlan reposted an article from The Cut on her Instagram Story with the headline "This Is a New Low for J.K. Rowling,” writing alongside it: "Keep your new ‘Harry Potter' lads. Wouldn't touch it with a 10 foot pole."

Rowling later claimed not to know who Coughlan was, nor “The Mandalorian” star Pedro Pascal, who has similarly criticized her views .

Representatives for Rowling and HBO did not immediately respond to Variety' s request for comment.

The news anchor and journalist is fronting Ancient Secrets with Erica Hill , a three-part series from CNN debuting next week.

The series from CNN Global Productions has been quietly shot, and CNN All Access subscribers can stream it from Monday, November 23.

The series will see CNN anchor and national correspondent Hill journey across some of the world's oldest landscapes and archeological sites to explore how humans go to today and what makes us who we are. The Best Feature Film Award "Golden Alexander – Theo Angelopoulos", accompanied by a 10,000-euro cash prize, was bestowed to the film : A Day in the Life of Jo: Chapter Phaedra by Jacqueline Lentzou The award was presented by Gaia Furrer, while director Jacqueline Lentzou took the stage to receive it. TELEKOM, the Festival Major Sponsor, supports the Best Director Award "Silver Alexander" with a cash prize of 5,000 euros. The award was bestowed to Pauline Julier & Nicolas Chapoulier for the film Les Indes The award was presented by Achilleas Kyriakidis. Reasoning: For the power of its cinematic vision and painterly landscapes, which transform a journey into the past into a visceral experience, revealing through its images the violence of power and the inequalities of the present. The Best Actor Award was jointly bestowed to : Caique Copque and Italo Martins for their performances in The Riverbank by Matheus Farias & Enock Carvalho The award was presented by Gaia Furrer. Reasoning: We are delighted to award Caique Copque and Italo Martins for the intensity and sensitivity of their performances and their extraordinary on-screen chemistry. Through their looks, gestures and physical presence, they make danger, desire, strength and vulnerability palpable. The Best Actress Award was bestowed to : Arisa Sasaki for her performance in Titanic Ocean by Konstantina Kotzamani The award was presented by Jack Tarling, while actress Arisa Sasaki took the stage to receive it. Reasoning: Between the weightlessness of water and the weight of growing up, Arisa Sasaki moved us with a performance of quiet intensity. She captures both the fragility and determination of a young woman finding her own voice in an environment that seems almost not of this world. The Artistic Achievement Award was bestowed to the film : Titanic Ocean by Konstantina Kotzamani The award was presented by Jack Tarling, while director Konstantina Kotzamani took the stage to receive it. Reasoning: Through the exceptional use of production design, costume, cinematography, sound design and music, Konstantina Kotzamani transports us into a mesmerizing, dark fantasy world. A visually stunning exploration of a controversial real way of life, with transcendental elements that take us even further beyond the world of our daily lives. A Special Mention was bestowed to : Evita Andriopoulou for her performance in A Day in the Life of Jo: Chapter Phaedra by Jacqueline Lentzou The distinction was presented by Achilleas Kyriakidis, while actress Evita Andriopoulou took the stage to receive it. Reasoning: Evita Andriopoulou captivated us with an understated naturalism and an emotional depth to her performance which took us on the intimate and unexpected journey of Jo. MEET THE NEIGHBORS+ AWARDS The Meet the Neighbors+ competition section includes debut or sophomore films from the 36 countries of Southeastern Europe, the Mediterranean and the Middle East. This year, the Municipality of Thessaloniki once again supports the Meet the Neighbors+ competition section with the new Municipality of Thessaloniki Best Screenplay Award, accompanied by a 5,000-euro cash prize. The jury is composed of: Sofia Exarchou (screenwriter and director) Anne Østerud (film editor) Cristina Cassano (Head of Contemporary Italian Cinema Promotion at Cinecittà S.p.A.) Jury members Sofia Exarchou, Anne Østerud and Cristina Cassano took the stage to present the awards. The Best Feature Film Award "Golden Alexander – Michel Demopoulos", accompanied by a 10,000-euro cash prize, was bestowed to the film : Dua , by Blerta Basholli The award was presented by Cristina Cassano. Reasoning: Dua stays with you long after the lights come up. Set in Pristina in the late 1990s, a thirteen-year-old girl searches for her place in a world that is changing too fast, in her own body and in the country around her, while the shadow of war grows closer. Blerta Basholli keeps the camera close to her young heroine and tells this coming-of-age story with restraint, honesty and deep humanity. This is a film about growing up while everything is breaking. For its emotional truth and its personal vision of a pivotal moment in Kosovo's history, the jury awards Best Film to Dua . The Best Director Award "Silver Alexander", accompanied by a 5,000-euro cash prize, was bestowed to Abdallah Al-Khatib for the film Chronicles from the Siege Reasoning: With a raw and deeply human approach that makes room for humour and absurdity, Abdallah Al-Khatib creates a film that becomes a revelatory and profoundly painful experience. The film is inspired by true stories of Palestinians, stories that represent only a very small part of the immense human tragedy unfolding in Palestine. In a land where fear, danger, and the threat of complete annihilation are constantly present, the director chooses to turn his gaze towards the people. Those who continue to move among the ruins, accompanied by the sounds of bombardment that recur with terrifying regularity. Those who insist on maintaining their daily routines and personal relationships. Those who insist on existing. The Silver Alexander, Best Director Award goes to Chronicles from the Siege and its director, Abdallah Al-Khatib. The award was presented by Sofia Exarchou, while Executive producer and Casting Director Lara Abul Failat took the stage to receive it. The Best Actor Award was jointly bestowed to : Alexis Manenti and Julian Świeżewski from the film Flesh and Fuel , by Pierre Le Gall The award was presented by Anne Østerud. Reasoning: Chasing a body, finding a human. From raw, pounding sex in stolen moments – sex we truly believe in – to the awkwardness, humour and unexpected tenderness of two men slowly letting down their guard. In Flesh and Fuel , Alexis Manenti and Julian Świeżewski walk straight into their roles, eyes wide open and with no vanity. Just naked, vulnerable bodies and warm, beating hearts. Manenti's guarded stillness meets Świeżewski's disarming openness. Together they create an electric chemistry that is as physical as it is deeply human. It is through their fearless, utterly exposed performances that this unexpected love story becomes so painfully real, leaving us just as vulnerable as the men on screen. The Best Actress Award was bestowed to : Maria Petrova from the film Hold Onto Me , by Myrsini Aristidou The award was presented by Sofia Exarchou, while actress Maria Petrova took the stage to receive it. Reasoning: In her first screen role, Maria Petrova gives a performance of rare truth as eleven-year-old Iris, who refuses to let her estranged father slip away again. Never leaning on sentiment, she builds the character through glances, silences, anger and tenderness. She reveals the inner world of a child suspended between innocence and the need to grow up. Director Myrsini Aristidou's camera stays close to her face, and Petrova holds that intimacy without a false note. Her chemistry with Christos Passalis anchors the film. For sincerity, emotional maturity and a magnetic screen presence, the jury awards Best Actress to Maria Petrova. The Best Screenplay Award sponsored by the Municipality of Thessaloniki, accompanied by a 5,000-euro cash prize, was bestowed to the film : Flesh and Fuel , by Pierre Le Gall Reasoning: "I see you. I see you." Who would have thought that two truck drivers passing on a bridge, calling out while honking their horns, could make us cheer like that? Five seconds of happiness. Flesh and Fuel 's screenplay turns a gritty workplace drama into a moving love story. It takes us from the loneliness of the road and brief, anonymous encounters to the surprise of falling in love, where Étienne and Bartosz's true obstacle isn't prejudice, but the harsh logistics of their industry. Told with brutality and humor, it is a wonderful story about finding connection in unlikely places". The Mayor of Thessaloniki, Stelios Angeloudis, took the stage to present the award and delivered a short address, while the winning film was announced by Anne Østerud. >>FILM FORWARD AWARDS The >>Film Forward competition section presents the work of new, daring filmmakers who, through their debut or sophomore films, challenge our relationship with reality and aspire to renegotiate it beyond the conventions of film genres. The jury is composed of: Ana Vujanović (researcher, writer, dramaturge and lecturer) Yorgos Zois (filmmaker) Carlos Rodríguez Ríos (director of D'A – Barcelona Film Festival) Jury member Carlos Rodríguez Ríos took the stage to present the awards. The Best Feature Film Award "Golden Alexander", accompanied by a 10,000-euro cash prize, was bestowed to the film : I Plant My Hand in the Garden by Boris Hadžija & Hoda Taheri Reasoning: The award for Best Film goes to I Plant My Hand in the Garden for its humor, emotionality, playing with social norms, and celebration of the diversity and fluidity of life. Drawing on their own struggles to obtain residence permits in Germany, the filmmaker duo from Serbia and Iran offer a mirror of European society that invites us to critically see ourselves in it. Artistically, the film transforms real life into fiction, while revealing the fictionality of life itself, both on screen and beyond. The Best Director Award "Silver Alexander", accompanied by a 5,000-euro cash prize, was bestowed to Rob Rice for the film Ponderosa Director Rob Rice took the stage to receive the award. Reasoning: The Best Director Award goes to Rob Rice for Ponderosa . The confidence and originality of his directorial vision are expressed through a distinctive visual style that stands out among more conventional directorial approaches. With its uncanny atmosphere, the awkwardness that permeates the performances and the unusual succession of scenes, the film creates a singular cinematic experience and approaches its characters with tenderness and love. The Best Actor Award was bestowed to : Alexis Kalofolias for his performance in Under the Judas Tree by Christos Houliaras Director Christos Houliaras took the stage to receive the award on behalf of Alexis Kalofolias. Reasoning: The award for Best Actor goes to Alexis Kalofolias for his sincere and thoughtful performance, which approaches the character without judgment, treating him instead with humanity, empathy and respect. The Best Actress Award was bestowed to : Alexis Bledel for her performance in Ponderosa by Rob Rice Director Rob Rice took the stage to receive the award on behalf of Alexis Bledel. Reasoning: The award for the best actress goes to Alexis Bledel for her delicate performance. With reduced but vibrant expressive means she depicts the depth of the character's inner world, which makes her interactions with the people around her plausible and convincing. Through her gaze she invites us to see the world, with all its fragility, pain and beauty. The Best Artistic Achievement Award was bestowed to the film : Particles of Dust by Argyris Germanidis Director Argyris Germanidis took the stage to receive the award. Reasoning: The Best Artistic Achievement Award goes to Particles of Dust , by Argyris Germanidis, for its inventive use of various image-making techniques and visual languages to explore a limbo world between spaces and times. A cinematic journey that awakens our cinephilia and connects us with our ghosts of the past and present.

articles.title: This Cult Superhero Franchise Will Keep Flopping Unless It Takes Cues From the Actual Comics Again
articles.summary: I have a soft spot for The Crow. There's something about that strange combination of supernatural horror and old-fashioned revenge that makes the character hard to forget. The original movie also gave us Brandon Lee in a role that still feels impossible to separate from his legacy. But here's something I've never quite understood. Why […]
articles.content:
James O'Barr's creation has explored some pretty unusual territory over the years. Different characters have taken up the mantle, and the stories have ventured into places that might surprise people who only know the movies. One particular comic even takes the supernatural revenge concept into the final days of World War II. That's a fascinating direction for a franchise that keeps struggling to find its identity beyond one beloved film. Maybe the problem isn't The Crow itself. Maybe Hollywood just needs to read a few more comics.

Here's a question. What if the next Crow movie didn't involve another musician getting murdered alongside his girlfriend? I know that's practically sacrilege when discussing a franchise built around one of the most recognizable revenge stories in comic book history. But James O'Barr has already explored other possibilities. Take The Crow: Skinning the Wolves . This three-issue miniseries from IDW takes place in a Nazi concentration camp in 1945. O'Barr returned to write the story and worked with artist Jim Terry to bring it to life. That's quite a departure from the familiar gothic atmosphere of Eric Draven's world. The setting also gives the supernatural mythology an entirely different kind of weight. O'Barr has discussed the difficulty of approaching such a horrific period without exploiting its history for entertainment. That's an important consideration when you're dealing with a story like this. And it's precisely the sort of creative ambition that could give the movies something genuinely different to explore.

And here's the trailer for the latest 2024 reboot, and it should be obvious why it was a failure and letdown.

The comics have never needed to limit themselves to Eric's particular tragedy. The Crow: Dead Time and The Crow: Flesh and Blood introduced other characters and explored different circumstances. That's the beauty of the concept—but also the one element that must be done in a such a way that won't feel too repetitive. The crow represents a supernatural force of vengeance rather than one particular person in black makeup. You can take that idea into another historical period or build an entirely different story around it. Imagine what a filmmaker could do with that freedom. We could get a period horror movie instead of another variation on the same modern revenge thriller. And honestly, wouldn't that be more interesting? Nobody needs another actor trying to recreate Brandon Lee's performance. That performance already belongs to the original movie. Let somebody else tell a story that stands on its own.

The original The Crow had something that Hollywood can't manufacture simply by hiring another director and putting an actor in white face paint. Alex Proyas understood the atmosphere of O'Barr's comic, and Brandon Lee gave Eric Draven a personality that made audiences care about him. The movie had romance, horror, humor, and some terrific action. Lee could look terrifying one minute and flash a mischievous grin the next. That's a big part of why the character worked. The sequels tried to continue the mythology with new protagonists. The Crow: City of Angels followed in 1996, then The Crow: Salvation arrived in 2000 and The Crow: Wicked Prayer followed in 2005. There was even a television series called The Crow: Stairway to Heaven . So the franchise certainly had opportunities to grow. The problem was that none of those follow-ups established the same lasting connection with audiences. Each tried to capture some of the original's appeal without giving the property a compelling identity of its own.

Then came the 2024 reboot . Once again Hollywood returned to Eric Draven and his tragic romance. I understand the temptation. The original movie remains beloved, and there's an obvious audience for another adaptation of O'Barr's creation. But going back to the same character doesn't automatically give us a reason to revisit the franchise. I'd much rather see a filmmaker take a chance on something like Skinning the Wolves . Give us a different era and a different protagonist. Let the supernatural mythology do some of the heavy lifting instead of asking audiences to compare every new performance with Lee's. The original The Crow will always be there for anyone who wants to revisit it. That's not going to change. But the comics have spent years showing that this world has more stories to tell. Maybe it's time the movies caught up.

French actor Gérard Depardieu has withdrawn his appeal against his conviction for sexually assaulting two women on the set of the 2021 film "Les Volets verts," making his 18-month suspended prison sentence final, according to French newspaper Le Monde.

articles.title: Poland’s Millennium Docs Against Gravity Reaches New Heights As World’s Second Biggest Nonfiction Film Festival
articles.summary: EXCLUSIVE: Millennium Docs Against Gravity has officially become the world’s second biggest documentary film festival, according to figures published by the cinematic event in Poland. The 23rd edition of MDAG, which took place in May this year, recorded 180,000 admissions, putting it just behind IDFA in Amsterdam in terms of audience. Growth has been dramatic […]
articles.content:
EXCLUSIVE: Millennium Docs Against Gravity has officially become the world's second biggest documentary film festival, according to figures published by the cinematic event in Poland.

The 23 rd edition of MDAG , which took place in May this year, recorded 180,000 admissions, putting it just behind IDFA in Amsterdam in terms of audience. Growth has been dramatic since the pandemic interregnum; in 2020, MDAG first passed the 100,000-attendee milestone.

MDAG's artistic director Karol Piekarczyk attributes the growth to "developing the audience and on listening to the audience and doing audience surveys. This is a very much festival that is in contact with audiences." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article1-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid","mid-articleX","mid-article","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[2,2],[300,250],[620,350],[300,251],[501,282],[3,3],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Podcast Doc Talk Podcast Goes Tête-À-Tête (À-Tête) With Leaders Of DC/DOX & Millennium Docs Against Gravity Documentary 'To Hold A Mountain,' 'A Fox Under A Pink Moon,' 'Mariinka' Among Big Winners At Millennium Docs Against Gravity In Poland

The groundwork for that success was laid in 2004 when festival director Artur Liebhart founded MDAG and simultaneously launched a distribution arm. Watch on Deadline if ( !window.pmc.harmony?.isEventAdScheduledTime() ) { pmcCnx.cmd.push(function() { pmcCnx({ settings: { plugins: { pmcAtlasMG: { iabPlcmt: 2, } } }, playerId: '32fe25c4-79aa-406a-af44-69b41e969e71', playlistId: '0199e506-e642-7728-8264-463efe71337b', }).render("connatix_contextual_player_div"); }); } else { // This should only be get called when page cache is not cleared and it's event time. window.pmc.harmony?.switchToHarmonyPlayer(); }

"When we started, there was really nothing. There was no documentary culture among the audience. There were no documentary feature films in the cinemas. That decision [was] to start from day one — the festival once a year and between the festivals to do theatrical releases — but at the same time also to show the opinion-making media and journalists, film critics, that this is something which is worth watching, worth checking out. Slowly but surely, the festival and theatrical distribution also changed the theatrical landscape in Poland. Now, when there is a new premiere of a documentary film every week in Poland, it's not a sensation anymore."

MDAG has cultivated a remarkably young audience. According to data on the festival website, the largest percentage of attendees in 2026 came in the 25-34 age range – 36-percent of the overall audience. Just over 60 percent of the audience fell in the 25-44 age range.

Beginning five years ago, the festival also built an industry program under Anna Szczypińska. That attracted 1,745 participants this year, an increase of 12.4 percent over 2025. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dl-mid-article-inject2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article2","mid-articleX","mid-article","mid","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

"We have never wanted to be another dot on the map that all the industry circles will just travel to," Liebhart comments. "We want to be that place that the industry comes to see how the [potential] of a documentary film can be seen in numbers, can be seen in a great audience of all ages which are entertained… So, we somehow made [the industry program] otherwise than most of the documentary festivals in the world."

What also makes MDAG unique among festivals is its reach. It unfolds in seven cities in Poland at the same time: Warsaw, Wrocław, Gdynia, Poznań, Katowice, Bydgoszcz, and Łódź. Each location features bespoke programming chosen from among the films accepted into the festival. "Because we are in so many cities," Piekarczyk told us in 2025, "there's over 1,200 screenings." Liebhart notes each location features Q&A sessions after screenings, "local juries and awards, as well as a wide range of accompanying events."

As evidence of MDAG's growing prominence, it has reached Oscar-qualifying status for Best Documentary Feature. "Further confirmation of its standing came through its partnership with FIPRESCI, the oldest and one of the most prestigious organizations representing film critics worldwide," according to a news release. "The federation chose MDAG to host its new award: the FIPRESCI Documentary Grand Prix. Starting in 2026, the award for the best documentary of the previous year has been presented at the festival's opening gala, with the winner selected through a vote by FIPRESCI members from around the world." (As Deadline reported , the inaugural prize went to Fiume o morte! directed by Igor Bezinović).

MDAG also takes an innovative approach to programming that goes beyond simply exhibiting a film. "Sometimes we take the music from the film to [perform] it live," Liebhart says. "Sometimes we discuss with a specialist after the screening from various points of view on what we have just seen on a big screen. So the documentary film of a high value is often the starting point for a wider discussion and for a wider kind of emotional scale."

Bank Millennium has been the festival's title sponsor for 21 years (hence the festival name Millennium Docs Against Gravity). Other supporters include the City of Warsaw, the Ministry of Culture and National Heritage, the European Union's MEDIA Program, the Polish Film Institute, and brands Visa and Canal+. The 2027 festival will take place from May 7–16 and online from May 18 to 31.

Goals for the festival going forward? "It would be great to have 200,000 [admission] next year," Piekarczyk shares. “But also for us, it's always important to keep the existing audiences happy. So, keep the level of the festival in terms of the quality of the films, events, really catering to what [people] want to see and what they need. I think growing audience-wise definitely, but also taking care of what we have."

Balancing innovation with audience satisfaction means, Piekarczyk says, "For us, the job is never boring."

articles.summary: Courtesy of The Walt Disney Company There are few movie trilogies where the final entry is better than anything that came before it, yet in the 1980s there were several examples of this including the then-final outing for Harrison Ford in Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade. After seeking out the Ark of the Covenant and avoiding voodoo priests, Indy's 1989 […]
articles.content:
Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade picked up the story of Indy in 1938, with the intrepid archeologist and adventurer discovering that his estranged father (played with ease by Sean Connery) has vanished while searching for the Grail. This leads to a globetrotting adventure for Indy as he attempts to follow the instructions in his father's diary and a rubbing from the Grail Tablet to save Henry Jones Sr. and beat Hitler's forces to the mythical item. The movie was directed by Steven Spielberg and produced by George Lucas, with Ford and Connery being joined by Alison Doody, Denholm Elliott, John-Rhys Davies, and River Phoenix. The movie was a return to form after the less-well received Temple of Doom , with the comedic bickering of Ford and Connery as the father and son duo being one of the most endearing qualities of the film. Making $474.2 million worldwide, Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade was the highest-grossing release of 1989.

The Last Crusade Grail Tablet is currently sitting on a bid of $10,000, but with 18 days to go that price could dramatically increase by the time the hammer finally falls on the auction. This is not the first time one of the several production made pieces has come up for sale in recent years, also sold by Heritage Auctions. The sale prices of these previous sales, which may or may not be the exact same item as the one currently up for grabs, are shown in the table below, which give an idea of what you could expect to pay if you decided to throw a bid in.

Yet even $25,000 is a small amount compared to some other Indy related items that have been sold in the last several years. The biggest seller ever was a 2024 sale of Harrison Ford's Temple of Doom Fedora which was bought for a massive $630,000, beating the 2018 $521, 362 sale of Ford's Raiders of the Lost Ark hat. Other big sales have included the Last Crusade and the Temple of Doom bullwhips, which respectively sold in July 2025 and March 2024 for $525,000 each. At the same March 2024 event, The Last Crusade ‘s hero Grail cup itself sold for $87,500. It is clear that the Grail Tablet is not going to reach those kind of highs, but could certainly outperform the previous sales.

How much would you pay to own a piece of Indiana Jones history? Is the Grail Tablet something you would add to your collection, or would a piece of Ford's iconic costume be better if money was no object? Let us know in the comments.

Autlook Filmsales, a leading sales agent for feature documentaries and doc series, has boarded Peter Alsted's "Dr. Hedgehog" ahead of the film's pitch at Forum, IDFA ‘s prestigious industry program. The Danish project is among the films selected for this year's Forum Pitch Presentations.

"Dr. Hedgehog" is a deep dive into the chaotic life of researcher Sophie Lund Rasmussen, the self-appointed Dr. Hedgehog. Rasmussen is the only Danish zoologist with a PhD in the small nocturnal animal and is on a mission to save the endangered creature while also battling 23 chronic illnesses. The project is produced by Denmark's Elk Film through producers Birgitte Keseler and Katrine Dolmer and executive producer Andreas Dalsgaard. Alsted's first documentary was 2015's award-winning "Standing on Water," with his films playing major festivals such as CPH:Dox.

Speaking with Variety ahead of the Forum, Autlook Filmsales's Stephanie Fuchs says the project "won us over right away." "It's tender, funny and surprising, and through this small creature, Peter says something big about care and our bond with the living world. We're thrilled to partner again with Elk Film and bring it to audiences worldwide.”

Alsted recalls meeting Rasmussen three years ago: "I read an article about her in the newspaper, and there was something about her that just caught my attention."

"There was, first of all, the little spiky animal that is endangered, but there were also her arms, which were tattooed with a list of her autoimmune diseases," he adds. "I contacted her and immediately kind of fell in love with her story, her character, her clumsy, nerdy, driven, passionate way of approaching life and her science. Also, at a time when there is so much fake news, she is dedicated to facts; she is data-driven." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

The director then went to one of her talks, where he saw her speak about her research on stage. He felt there was a creative "chemistry," and proposed the idea of the film right away. Rasmussen was not only open but greatly enthusiastic about sharing her research and life on screen, with the two spending the first year of their collaboration getting to know each other better and filming kicking off last year.

Alsted believes "Dr. Hedgehog" has great potential to "resonate with the everyday person." He mentions how Rasmussen defines the hedgehog as "the perfect bridge between wildlife and modern society, because they live in our backyards." "They are right outside our door, and they're the easiest wild animal to get close to because they just curl up."

There is also the fact that Rasmussen is a personable character, someone with a great life purpose but also open about her daily struggles. "She has 23 diagnosed chronic illnesses and her health has been deteriorating since she was four years old. She has a death stamp on her, and I think this speaks to a lot of people who are in similar situations, struggling with either their physical or mental health, and who can't relate to people like Elon Musk or a big, rich celebrity."

Keseler was immediately drawn to the project upon first hearing about Rasmussen's story from Alsted. She and the team at Elk Films boarded "Dr. Hedgehog" right away, and first introduced the project to the market at Nordisk Panorama in September.

"We had such great feedback and a lot of interest," she says of the experience. "We were nervous, of course, but we got feedback that the film is hopeful, that it's dealing with something people can connect to. The film is coming at a time when the world is shifting into a horrible place, and Sophie brings a little hope because she's this regular person who has a lot of challenges but still does something to improve her space and therefore all of our spaces."

The "Dr. Hedgehog" team is hoping to secure the means to start full production in spring of 2027, with expected completion at the end of 2028. When asked if they feel a certain sense of urgency given the scientist's unpredictable illnesses, Alsted says: "The sense of urgency also comes from her because she wants us to finish the film so she can actually watch it [laughs]. It's definitely a thing. She calls me, texts me any time she is doing something, so we have a lot of trust, but she also definitely wants me to finish the film [laughs]." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Gérard Depardieu has announced he is abandoning plans to appeal a sexual assault verdict and 18-month suspended meted out to him earlier this year in relation to events on the set of Jean Becker's The Green Shutters in 2021.

"The justice system has spoken. I have been found guilty. I accept this, and I take full responsibility for the conviction,” the French star wrote in a statement entitled "I hear" and sent to local media.

The sentence comes eight months after a high-profile and tumultuous trial in Paris in March in which Depardieu was found guilty of groping two women on the set of The Green Shutters . His declaration renders the verdict and sentence, handed out in May, final. "On film sets, I long hid behind provocation and crude, suggestive humor,” continued the statement. "I believed my comments and actions to be without consequence. They were not, given they were coming from a powerful person such as myself at the time… I now understand that there is a boundary between impertinence and offence. I never intended hurting the women whose paths I crossed, but I understand that intention does not change the hurt. " “This story has caused a lot of suffering. articles.title: Piv Bernth, Producer of ‘The Killing,' and ’Babylon Berlin’ Creators Win Honorary Awards at Tallinn’s TV Beats Forum
articles.summary: Trailblazing international TV figures Piv Bernth, producer of “The Killing” and “The Bridge,” and “Babylon Berlin” creators Achim von Borries, Tom Tykwer and Henk Handloegten are the recipients of this year’s TV Beats Honorary Awards. Granted by the TV Beats Forum, the drama series strand of Industry@Tallinn & Baltic Event, the industry arena of the […]
articles.content:
Trailblazing international TV figures Piv Bernth , producer of "The Killing" and "The Bridge," and " Babylon Berlin " creators Achim von Borries , Tom Tykwer and Henk Handloegten are the recipients of this year's TV Beats Honorary Awards.

Granted by the TV Beats Forum , the drama series strand of Industry@Tallinn & Baltic Event, the industry arena of the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival , the Awards saw Von Borries pick up one Sunday night in Tallinn on behalf of the "Babylon Berlin" team. TV Beats will host a Fireside Chat with the honorees on Nov. 16. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories From 'Dil Se' to 'Ramayana': How Indian Cinema Shattered the U.K., Ireland Box Office Glass Ceiling 'Ramayana' Makes History as First Indian Film to Top U.K., Ireland Box Office as 'Godzilla Minus Zero' Debuts in Third

Both awards go to seminal figures whose shows are not just series but symbols of a new industrial era, step-ups of global audience interest in non-English series.

Bernth's producing credits at Danish public broadcaster DR include the International Emmy-winning "Nikolaj and Julie" (2002-03) and "The Killing" (2007-12) while she her executive producer credits include "The Bridge" (2011-18) and "1864" (2014). As DR's Head of Drama, she also commissioned acclaimed series including "The Legacy" (2014-17) and "Follow the Money" (2016-19).

While "The Bridge" is the touchstone of Nordic Noir, "Wallander" was the first Nordic procedural to premiere on BBC4, in November 2008. It was "The Killing," however, premiering on BBC4 in Spring 2011, which really opened the dam gates of Nordic Noir in international, winning a BAFTA and Intl. Emmy and setting a blueprint for the sub-genre, positing crime fiction whose focus is not just the investigation but its consequences or context, a complexity of character rare in international crime series and a serialized case which with "The Killing's" first murder case went on for 20 episodes. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Few series have depicted better the across-the-board madness of war – psychological, military, political and social – than "1864."

In 2017, Bernth co-founded Apple Tree Productions with Lars Hermann, subsequently acquired by ITV Studios, which produced Netflix hit "Equinox" and, notably, "Blackwater" (2023) a suspense-powered double murder mystery and the portrait of a community fighting oblivion, whether the impunity of murders, or older communities and ways of life dying out, or the fading of memory.

"Few producers have changed international expectations of Nordic television drama as profoundly as Piv Bernth,"said Petri Kemppinen and Roosa Toivonen, co-heads of TV Beats Forum.

"Through her work as a producer, executive producer and drama commissioner, she has championed complex characters, creative risk-taking and stories that resonate far beyond their country of origin."

The TV Beats Award comes at what could be seen as part of an end of an era, with Bernth and Apple TV Productions co-founder Lars Hermann announcing late last year that they will shutter the production house at the end of 2026. "The market for making TV series is becoming increasingly difficult in Denmark, and it has become ever more challenging to maintain and build an economically viable business," Bernth and Hermann said in a statement.

‘Babylon Berlin' creators Achim von Borries, Tom Tykwer and Henk Handloegten

Six years later, with Netflix having launched over Europe, local pay TV players and broadcasters hit back. Charting through 48 hours of fiction the history of Weimar Germany from the end of WW1 in 1918 to the rise to power of the Nazi Party in March 1933 from the point of view of its leads, police inspector Gereon Rath (Volker Bruch) and clerk Charlotte Ritter (Liv Lisa Fries), "Babylon Berlin" premiered Oct. 13, 2017 on Sky 1.

Doing so, it belongs to a remarkable Golden Age last four months of 2017 when Netflix and rivals launched some of the biggest swings in their history, supercharged by a feeding fever for big signature non-English-language premium plays: Netflix bowed "Dark" Dec. 1 2017, and a recut version of Spain's "La Casa de Papel," called "Money Heist," on Dec. 20. All stand out for their enormous artistic ambition, and in the case of "Babylon Berlin," its extraordinary period production levels. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

The TV Beats Honorary Awards to Tykwer, von Borries and Handloegten coincide with the launch of Berlin Babylon's fifth and final season on German public broadcast ARD on Sept. 10.

“It was a wonderful experience. Sometimes painful but mainly wonderful. I grew tremendously creatively through this period, as we all did. It was for us three probably the biggest enterprise we ever made. Like a 48h long film! It sounds crazy,” von Borries said in Tallinn, accepting the TV Beats Honorary Award.

“There was a natural ending that everybody had heard about: 1933, when Hitler came to power,” he continued, talking of Season 5.

“Also, we thought we would never portray Hitler and end it in January [1933], when he was announced as Chancellor of Germany. We realised,however, that it was just the beginning of the end. We therefore focused on Feb 1933. This season shows how easy it is to destroy things and how difficult it is to rebuild."

"When ‘ Babylon Berlin' launched in 2017, a German-language period drama competing with the biggest English-language series was an extraordinarily ambitious proposition. Tom Tykwer, Achim von Borries and Henk Handloegten had the vision and courage to make it happen," said Kemppinen and Toivonen.

"Their work has shown that language is no barrier to international success and that European series can set the standard for premium drama. We are delighted to honour the creative partnership behind this remarkable series," they added.

TV Beats Forum takes run over Nov. 15-17 in Tallinn. Industry@Tallinn & Baltic Event rans as one of North Europe's key film-TV platforms gathering executives and creatives most especially from Baltics, Central Eastern Europe and the Nordic converge to collaborate.

Annika Pham contributed to this article.

articles.title: 5 Notoriously Hated ‘90s Movies That Are Actually Worth Watching, Including 1 That Killed A Superhero Franchise
articles.summary: With the sheer number of movies released each calendar year, it's clear that not every film can be universally beloved. For every truly great movie, there is always one or two that aren't particularly good — that is to say, that they don't really strike a chord with critics or audiences. While even the worst […]
articles.content:
To put it plainly, even notoriously hated movies can be worth watching . Recently, we looked at specific examples of this particular phenomenon from the 2000s, but the decade before also featured many such movies. While each of the following films has gone down in history as a major disaster and a movie that deserves to be forgotten, they're all still worth watching for one reason or another, proving to be enjoyable in their own unique ways.

Waterworld is one of the most notorious box office disappointments of all time, and that unfortunate accolade has contributed to a pretty poor reputation. The 1995 movie stars Kevin Costner as the Mariner, a nameless antihero who sails the Earth of the far future, which has been devastated by the melting of the polar ice caps, covering almost its entire surface with water. As well as being unable to recoup its massive budget, Waterworld was nominated for multiple Golden Raspberry Awards, which did nothing to help its reputation. Not only did the movie not deserve its Worst Picture Razzie nomination , but Waterworld has been severely underrated ever since its release. There's no denying that the movie has some issues, but the sheer scope and ambition of the film remain impressive, and its story delivers fun post-apocalyptic action. Its reputation as a disappointing movie confuses financial performance with its ability to entertain, and despite being widely despised, Waterworld is actually well worth seeing at least once.

Cutthroat Island is widely remembered for only one reason. Having gone down in history as one of the biggest box office bombs of all time, the movie is infamous for having caused its studio, Carolco Pictures, to cease operations. The 1995 movie is a swashbuckling action adventure whose massive budget and troubled production ultimately set it up to fail. Starring Geena Davis and Matthew Modine, the movie's story of a female pirate chasing after a legendary treasure sounds like the plot of a potentially epic adventure movie. For all of its issues, Cutthroat Island is just what it appears to be: a throwback to an era of action-adventure films that has been all but forgotten, with many impressive practical effects that have seen it age remarkably well. It's another film whose financial performance has negatively affected its reputation, but this does Cutthroat Island no justice whatsoever. Generally speaking, the movie is only hated because of its reputation, as it's actually an incredibly enjoyable piece of mid-'90s cinema that truly deserves more love.

While there are some examples of movies from the 1990s that are unfairly hated, The Postman is not one of them. With a runtime just short of three hours, The Postman tried to deliver a post-apocalyptic epic, but the absurdity of its premise got in the way. It follows Kevin Costner as a nomad who discovers a United States Postal Service uniform and begins to deliver mail across the ravaged society of its imagined future. The problem with The Postman is that it tried so hard to deliver an earnest tale of hope and restoration, but the sheer ridiculousness of its central idea made it impossible. It lacks the lingering sense of realism that runs through all the best post-apocalyptic movies , instead abandoning them in favor of a premise that is practically laughable. Despite being widely hated for its self-seriousness, The Postman is still worth watching for fans of apocalyptic movies, albeit with one simple caveat: be willing to laugh at the movie, rather than with it. It's not a funny film, but its desire to be treated seriously is inherently comedic, making it well worth watching despite its many shortcomings.

1997's Batman & Robin was the second of Joel Schumacher's Batman movies , and also proved to be not just the director's last attempt at a Batman movie, but the hero's final big-screen outing for nearly a decade. Batman Forever took the DC movie franchise in a new, more family-friendly direction, and Batman & Robin went even further. The result was a campy superhero flick that seemed to suffer from a bizarre identity crisis, resulting in a reputation that it still has yet to recover from. The film's many ideas about adapting Batman and his supporting characters were widely ridiculed, but some of its reputation is undeserved. It may be the worst Batman movie out there, but it's still a passable superhero film. Its campy elements and terrible one-liners make it a deliciously cheesy popcorn flick, and while many claim to hate it, it continues to pop up in conversations about the Dark Knight's cinematic history. When it comes to superhero cinema, Batman & Robin is a true guilty pleasure movie that, while not a particularly good film, still deserves to be treated a little better than it usually is.

There are a handful of 1990s comic book movies that are widely considered some of the worst in the genre's history, and 1995's Judge Dredd is often listed among them. Starring Sylvester Stallone as the iconic eponymous lawman, the adaptation of the 2000 AD character was underwhelming in many ways, to say the least. It played fast and loose with many important aspects of the character from the source material, alienating many fans in the process. This, combined with negative reviews and an underwhelming box office take, led to Judge Dredd going down in history as a widely hated '90s movie. However, even as a fan of the comics, there are elements of the 1995 film that deserve more praise. The worldbuilding and tone of the film were closer to the source material than they get credit for, and Stallone's apparent lack of self-awareness in the role felt bizarrely apt in many ways. Judge Dredd is, by no stretch of the imagination, a good film, but despite being widely hated by many, it's still worth watching as another '90s guilty pleasure movie.
