articles.title: Tom Cruise Has Only Made 2 Horror Movies in 45 Years, and the Best Is This '90s Gem
articles.summary: The poster boy for American action stars, Tom Cruise has spent the majority of his career inside larger-than-life worlds, playing the hero. Starting early with Top Gun and Days of Thunder and eventually landing his most famous contract with the Mission: Impossible franchise, Cruise’s typical silver-screen persona is confident and good-natured, with unyielding strength in […]
articles.content:
But what about his best horror performance? A case could be made for War of the Worlds , although its action-adventure elements still dominate. This leaves only Cruise’s 1994 role in Neil Jordan's adaptation of Anne Rice's novel Interview with the Vampire as his most notable horror performance. Cruise stars as the charismatic vampire Lestat alongside a young Kirsten Dunst as Claudia and Brad Pitt as Louis de Pointe du Lac, who recounts his centuries-long life as a vampire to Christian Slater’s journalist. Yet despite the stacked cast, Cruise remains the film's standout, particularly because he takes his leading-man reputation and turns it on its head.

Before Interview with the Vampire , Cruise had already established his reputation through performances in Top Gun , Rain Man , Born on the Fourth of July , A Few Good Men , and The Firm . In the early 90s, he was increasingly moving towards serious dramatic roles but still favored sympathetic leading characters. Not only was Lestat de Lioncourt a substantial departure from the good-guy image, but it didn’t fit squarely into either action or prestige drama. At the time of his casting, the disconnect was so great that author Anne Rice publicly objected to Cruise playing Lestat. She considered him an incorrect choice for the aristocratic, flamboyant vampire she’s created. She roasted the decision in the press, calling it “the worst crime in the name of casting since The Bonfire of the Vanities” and “so bizarre, it's almost impossible to imagine how it's going to work.”

Yet Cruise shocked the world by not only giving us a fantastic Lestat, but also delivering the best performance in the film. Even Rice came around after seeing the movie, placing a self-funded two-page ad in The New York Times apologizing for her earlier public criticism of Cruise's casting , stating, “I never dreamed it would turn out this way.” As Rice and many critics of the time noted, Cruise’s Lestat works so well not despite his public persona, but precisely because of it, using his leading-man charm to make Lestat more convincing to both the characters and the audience. Lestat’s handsome confidence and humor are offset beautifully when he is revealed as a remorseless killer who treats human beings as disposable, using seduction as his weapon of choice.

The complexities Cruise communicates through Lestat are incredible. When Lestat offers Louis the opportunity to become a vampire, he promises him the choice he himself was denied, and the restraint with which Cruise delivers the line lets the character's loneliness peek through the veneer. Simultaneously, the offer is manipulative: Lestat wants a companion and sees Louis as someone who can fill that role. Is the vulnerability real or part of the manipulation? Therein lies the brilliance of Cruise’s performance, which only becomes more openly cruel as Louis struggles with his new existence. Perhaps most unsettling is when Lestat turns Dunst's Claudia (another standout performance) into a vampire and presents her as their new daughter, intending the unconventional family arrangement to solve their problems. Cruise's enthusiasm and excitement at having condemned a child to an eternity is genuinely horrifying.

Though critics were initially mixed upon the film’s release, the movie received two technical Oscar nominations: Best Art Direction and Best Original Score. Interview with the Vampire has since accrued a dedicated cult following among genre movie lovers. For all its camp and melodrama, the movie remains genuinely emotionally devastating, thanks in part to the nuance Cruise brings to the screen. A satisfying mix of horror, romance, and drama with doomed blood-suckers at its center, Interview With the Vampire deserves recognition among the genre's finest films.

While Cruise's performance is a major reason Interview with the Vampire holds up, the film's timelessness also comes from its execution. Neil Jordan whips up an elaborate gothic world stretching from New Orleans to Paris with help from production designer Dante Ferretti, cinematographer Philippe Rousselot, and composer Elliot Goldenthal. As for the ensemble, Pitt gives Louis a melancholy that plays beautifully off Lestat's flamboyance, while 11-year-old Dunst delivers an extraordinary early-career performance as Claudia, even earning her a Golden Globe nomination (she apparently lost the win by a single vote). Antonio Banderas, Stephen Rea, and Christian Slater round out the stellar cast.

In 2022, the AMC TV adaptation of Interview with the Vampire also received critical acclaim. Starring Sam Reid, Jacob Anderson, and Bailey Bass, the series supposedly took substantial liberties with Rice's original story . Rice and her son Christopher were involved in the series' development. However, she died before its premiere, making it impossible to know how she would have responded to the changes or finished adaptation—or whether another smear campaign or two-page apology ad would have been in order. Both versions have their merits, but with the Rice seal of approval, Neil Jordan's 1994 film remains the definitive adaptation of Interview with the Vampire in which Tom Cruise gives one of the most distinctive performances of his career and, to date, his finest work in horror.

Do you consider Interview with the Vampire to be one of the great vampire movies? Let us know in the comments below.

SPOILER ALERT: The following story contains plot details from "Ain't That Good News," Season 4, Episode 3 of " The Gilded Age ," now streaming on HBO Max.

Peggy Scott's happily ever after was years in the making.

"That's always been the really long game, intentional pursuit that I've been on with the show," says Denée Benton, the actor who portrays the enterprising secretary turned journalist turned novelist — and now, bride! — on HBO's "The Gilded Age." In an accurate reflection of the 19th century, Peggy has been handed some of the heaviest material on Julian Fellowes' hit period drama. But Benton has also advocated for her character to partake in some of the lush fantasy that otherwise pervades the show. And starting with last season's meet-cute with handsome doctor William Kirkland (Jordan Donica), Peggy did.

This Sunday, Peggy and William's romance reached its zenith with the couple's wedding, one of the most emotional and cathartic scenes "The Gilded Age" has produced to date. Benton namechecks Emmy-winning production designer Bob Shaw, costume designer Kasia Walicka-Maimone and producing director Salli Richardson Whitfield with bringing Peggy's walk down the aisle to life. "They did us such justice with how stunning it all looks. The amount of background that it took to fill that church, and to shoot in a church from that time with the stained Tiffany glass and the light shining in — it made the whole room have this warm glow."

Peggy and William's nuptials aren't just a hard-won moment for the couple themselves. As written by Fellowes and executive producer Sonja Warfield, who share credit on the season's scripts, the wedding is loaded with the significance of a Black couple forming a family just a couple of decades after the Civil War. (Both of Peggy's parents are formerly enslaved.) Theater veteran Adrienne Warren becomes the latest Tony winner to grace "The Gilded Age" as Peggy's cousin Ava, whose gift is to serenade her and William as part of the Jubilee Singers, a real-life a cappella ensemble who sang spirituals developed under slavery for post-emancipation audiences.

After a tense back-and-forth with William's mother Elizabeth (Phylicia Rashad) — more on that shortly — Peggy and William also partake in the ritual of jumping over a broom together, another holdover from an era when slavery prevented Black couples from staging more elaborate celebrations. "Salli and I were kind of in a loving conspiracy together about like — OK, this cannot be a quick montage," Benton says of the broom jump, which is ultimately presented in slow motion. "This needs to be the historical TV moment that it really is. HBO was really on board to make sure that we carved out enough space for it, because I really think audiences are going to be moved in ways that they don't expect. They're seeing something new — not something that didn't exist, but something that hasn't been framed." Related Stories Dolly Parton's Last Recorded Song Released: Listen to Her Passionate Performance on U2's 'Torn' U2 Gets On Its Boots for First All-New Full-Length Record in Nine Years, 'Carnaval de Luz,' With More Callbacks to Band's '90s Peaks Than '80s Glories: Album Review

Benton is acutely aware of what it means for Peggy to experience the same rite of passage as wealthy white characters like Gladys Russell (Taissa Farmiga), whose marriage to a duke was a major storyline last season. (In fact, William and Peggy are the first true love match we see tie the knot on "The Gilded Age," since Gladys and the duke's union was arranged.) "It really legitimizes Peggy as one of the romantic leads of the show," Benton says. "It's like, this is a character we are now loudly naming and investing in." Peggy also has a thriving career, but starring in a marriage plot cements her as a true heroine of this Edith Wharton-inspired universe. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

When Elizabeth tries to veto the broom, Peggy stands her ground, draws a boundary and firmly puts her now mother-in-law in her place.

"As an actor, that scene made me so much better," Benton says of sharing the screen with Rashad. "It was like eating candy and steak all at the same time." Peggy is a kind and decent person, but her showdown with Elizabeth also shows her sharper edge: "What I love about that scene is, it's very elite shade," Benton observes. In addition to Warfield and Whitfield, Benton credits historian and co-executive producer Dr. Erica Dunbar and executive producer Davita Scarlett, a new addition to the writing team in Season 4, for shaping Peggy's arc. "What's really special is that Season 4 feels like it's even more Peggy's season than Season 3 was," Benton says of the collective effort to craft a multifaceted Black heroine who gets to have her accomplishments and her escapism alike. Yes, enslaved people were doing that, but in that time post emancipation, they really weren't, because then they could legally be married and so the tradition came back really in the 20th century," Warfield continued. "We got to take some poetic license, artistic license and keep it because we were trying some other things, but really it needed to be that because that represents the division between the families," Warfield said. "Elizabeth does not want to remember anything from enslavement period, while Peggy wants to pay homage to her family, to her dad and her parents. It is completely like diametrically opposed. Another wrinkle in the plans for the nuptials comes in the form of the Fisk Jubilee singers, led by Dorothy and Peggy's cousin Ava (Adrienne Warren), who attends Peggy's pre-wedding tea and announces that she's brought the choir to sing hymns at the ceremony in Newport, Rhode Island. Elizabeth is not fond of this idea either, nor, at first, is her husband (Brian Stokes Mitchell), who ultimately presides over Peggy and William's ceremony. Much like in the show, this addition was not originally in the plans for Season 4's third episode.

"I believe Sally [Richardson Whitfield] talked to Dr. [Erica] Dunbar because Sally wanted to add more to the wedding, which I was all for. At first, we had to be budget conscious, but then we got some more budget, so then we were able to add the Fisk Jubilee singers," Warfield said. "I thought it need[ed] to be important to Peggy in a meaningful way, and so then we get to introduce cousin Ava as one of the singers."

Warfield described the broom as something "tangible" to be angry about regarding Peggy instead of just saying she doesn't like her soon-to-be daughter-in-law, giving actress Phylicia Rashad plenty of opportunities to "annihilate just with a look." Meanwhile, the defensiveness Dorothy feels for her daughter is just one of many emotions on the big day.

"Dorothy is more than proud; there's probably everything in it. There's pride. There's relief. There's joy. There's a little sadness because she has to let go. She's got to let go in a way that she hasn't had to. [Dorothy] probably had more time to cling to [Peggy] because of Peggy's setting out on her own in the beginning, and so all of that is swirled into one," McDonald told Deadline. "In some ways she starts to feel a little more nostalgic for and a little more romance toward Arthur again. They feel more like a unit now, given how separated they all were in Seasons 1 and 2. So, to see that bond come back together, she's feeling that, and Peggy is finally getting the joy that she deserves. She's emerging into this powerful young modern Black woman. That's a fulfilling thing to see. Her ancestors are definitely smiling down on her."

"She's wearing the crown that her ancestors bought and paid for. So that's a lot of beautiful things come to fruition. In some ways, it may be why Dorothy is so stringent and so unwilling to back down about the broom," McDonald continued. "That's honoring the ancestors. Like ‘Yes, you did buy and pay for this crown, and we are honoring you and saying we see you, we thank you, and we give gratitude to and we remember you. That's why I think Dorothy's willing to do a knockdown, hat-pulling, hair-pulling fight to get to this moment. That's why it's such a beautiful moment when it happens."

In an interview paired with McDonald, co-star Cynthia Nixon called Peggy's wedding "the wedding to end all weddings” and she traced the other ceremonies that have speckled The Gilded Age so far.

"Every one is different. We've had Gladys's wedding with the bride sobbing down the aisle . We've had Enid's and Oscar's wedding, which is sort of hilarious. We've had Ada and Luke's wedding, which is late in life and full of anguish because you think Agnes isn't going to come, and it's more small and modest," she said. "The wedding of Peggy and Dr. Kirkland, is this fruition of this tremendous love and the most opulent and beautiful, but also heartfelt and full of tradition and singing and the beautiful attire and the stained glass, and it just it is the apex of all the weddings we've ever had on the show." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-articleX","mid-article","btf","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() ; });

"The days that we were shooting it, because it took a long time to shoot, it was the night that the Knicks won. So, we literally had to stop shooting for a while to watch those final moments," the Tony winner said. "Everybody was stationed at phones and Sally Richardson was like, ‘We can't keep going. Let's turn on some TVs.' And we're all watching, and then screaming our heads off for I don't know how late it was. And then we went back to finishing the wedding. We did end up watching the sunrise that night, but it was a worthy night. It was kind of magical that it happened on the night of the of the wedding."

articles.title: 'Downstate' Broadway Review: Provocative Play About Sex Offenders Questions The Nature Of Forgiveness
articles.summary: Among many other things, Downstate, Bruce Norris' tricky new play that's gained considerable acclaim and controversy, is an exercise in cognitive dissonance, a commandingly written and shrewdly directed (by Joe Mantello) work that asks us to confront some of the very things we prize most in ourselves, namely the limits of our compassion and empathy. […]
articles.content:
Among many other things, Downstate , Bruce Norris ‘ tricky new play that's gained considerable acclaim and controversy, is an exercise in cognitive dissonance, a commandingly written and shrewdly directed (by Joe Mantello ) work that asks us to confront some of the very things we prize most in ourselves, namely the limits of our compassion and empathy.

Set in a shabby, cheaply furnished middle-class home we're told is located in downstate Illinois, the play immediately introduces us to the house's residents: four middle-aged men who bicker over who owes what for the week's groceries, personal belongings left in common spaces and other petty irritations of daily, group living. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article1-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid","mid-articleX","mid-article","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[2,2],[300,250],[620,350],[300,251],[501,282],[3,3],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories News Steve Carell & John C. Reilly To Star In 'The Odd Couple' Broadway Revival This Spring Casting Jessica Chastain Returning To Broadway In New Play 'Lost Lear'; Corey Stoll, Michael Urie Co-Star

And we're also introduced to a younger man, maybe in his 30s, who is nervous and uncomfortable. Andy (Thomas Sadoski) has come to confront the most frail of the group home residents: Fred (Francis Guinan), an aging, vaguely confused man in a wheelchair – we learn why he is so confined later – who has something terrible in common with his housemates: He is a convicted sex offender and child predator who has officially served his time in prison but, with no where to go, is living in this group home under strict observation and restrictions. Watch on Deadline if ( !window.pmc.harmony?.isEventAdScheduledTime() ) { pmcCnx.cmd.push(function() { pmcCnx({ settings: { plugins: { pmcAtlasMG: { iabPlcmt: 2, } } }, playerId: '32fe25c4-79aa-406a-af44-69b41e969e71', playlistId: '0199e506-e642-7728-8264-463efe71337b', }).render("connatix_contextual_player_div"); }); } else { // This should only be get called when page cache is not cleared and it's event time. window.pmc.harmony?.switchToHarmonyPlayer(); }

Fred is a former piano teacher, Andy his former student and you can probably guess the rest. It's been 30 years since Fred sexually assaulted Andy on two separate occasions, and the former student's life has been a shambles of shame, depression and struggle ever since. Andy's wife, Em (Cassie Beck), is by his side for moral support as he attempts to finally face his abuser with a list of the crimes and their impact on his life. Em, too, has a list, its very existence an indication of how abuse spreads well beyond the first victim.

Sharing the home (flawlessly designed by the ever-reliable Scott Pask) with Fred are Dee (K. Todd Freeman), an aging Black gay man and a sort of de facto house mother who does the grocery shopping, makes sure Fred takes his pills and nags Gio (Al'Jaleel McGhee), the youngest of the group, to move his gym equipment out of the common area. Gio, talkative, aggressively friendly and very funny – somehow, Downstate has an improbable amount of genuine humor – holds himself above his housemates, convinced that the relatively advanced age of his victim – she was 17 – bestows on him a moral superiority and a brighter future. It does neither, particularly after he shows up with a new, clueless young friend (Ivy Wolk). blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dl-mid-article-inject2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article2","mid-articleX","mid-article","mid","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Finally, there's Felix (Adrian Martinez), the quietest, most antisocial and, frankly, most outwardly pathetic of the bunch, lonely, morosely religious, secretive and resentful at having to live with people he disdains. It's Felix who seems to draw the most attention and concern from Ivy ( The Bear ‘s Liza Colón-Zayas), the visiting probation officer who keeps all the men under a watchful eye and whose initial conviviality can't mask the seriousness with which she takes both her job and the crimes the men in her charge have committed.

Playwright Norris (he wrote the excellent Clybourne Park ) builds the tension and momentum of Downstate almost entirely through character interaction – it's only in retrospect that we realize there hasn't been much by way of plot, or at least action, in what we've just witnessed – and yet the entire play is compelling from beginning to end. We watch as Dee, the most outwardly compassionate and intelligent of the bunch, gradually shows his meaner side, and Gio, for all his lip service to self-improvement and goal-setting, constantly puts himself (and others) in danger. Sad Felix, whose denials of rule-breaking we want to believe, at last gives us no choice but to acknowledge the worst.

And make no doubt, what these characters do, and are capable of, is the worst . Prior to Broadway, Downstate had productions in Washington D.C., Off Broadway, London and at Chicago's Steppenwolf, drawing some right-wing ire – after a positive review in the Washington Post, Ted Cruz tweeted, “So now the corporate media is praising pedophilia” – but those reactions couldn't be more wrong-headed. True, Downstate insists that we see and consider the humanity of these men, but that is most certainly not the same as asking us to excuse their crimes. Downstate dares us to forgive the unforgivable, challenging the very concept of grace.

“Praising pedophilia?” Nonsense. If anything, I came away from Downstate entirely convinced that not one of these four characters should live unrestricted among society. Age and infirmity has rendered Fred the former piano teacher somewhat harmless, though his blithe, ostensibly sympathetic demeanor around the still-devastated Andy speaks volumes. Dee, so fiercely protective of Fred, still harbors delusions that excuse his crime, a rationalizing that masks itself as intellectual debate but even that falls to the side when his cruelty and destructiveness surface. The fates of Gio and Felix might be shocking, but not surprising.

Director Mantello guides his excellent cast through Downstate ‘s nuances subtly ands unerringly, with the performers creating fully credible characters cursed by – whose to say? – trauma or demons or nature. What Downstate leaves us with, then, is both understanding and the limits of understanding, the frustration of somehow wanting to forgive but knowing that forgiveness can't provide these victimizers what they crave: A home in the world, a place that isn't a four-bedroom prison with crummy furniture and an ankle bracelet.

Title: Downstate Venue: Broadway's Booth Theatre Written By: Bruce Norris Directed By: Joe Mantello Cast: K. Todd Freeman, Francis Guinan, Thomas Sadoski, Al'Jaleel McGhee, Cassie Beck, Adrian Martinez, Ivy Wolk, Liza Colón-Zayas Running Time: 2 hr 20 min (including intermission)

articles.title: Spider-Man's Most Important Movie Scene Isn't One With Superhero Costumes or Explosions
articles.summary: Superhero movies are known for their big moments. Somebody discovers their powers, a villain reveals an evil plan, or an entire city gets demolished. Sam Raimi's Spider-Man has plenty of those necessary tropes. There's the Green Goblin causing chaos, Peter Parker swinging through New York, and Willem Dafoe playing one of Marvel's most devious villains. […]
articles.content:
It sounds pretty harmless, doesn't it? Peter Parker , Aunt May, Mary Jane Watson, Harry Osborn, and Norman Osborn gather around the table for a holiday meal. There's food, awkward conversation, and the usual family tension. Yet something rather important happens during that dinner. Norman starts putting the pieces together about Peter's secret identity, and suddenly an ordinary family gathering becomes one of the most uncomfortable scenes in the entire movie. Raimi understood that sometimes the scariest thing a villain can do is simply sit across from you in a seemingly normal situation.

There's a lot going on during this seemingly ordinary meal. Peter has been trying to balance his responsibilities as Spider-Man with his increasingly complicated personal life. He's also getting closer to Mary Jane, which doesn't exactly make things easier with his best friend Harry. Then there's Norman Osborn, who arrives carrying plenty of his own problems. Willem Dafoe is particularly good here because Norman can still play the charming businessman when he wants to. He's Harry's father, Peter's employer, and a respected figure in their little social circle. Nobody at the table knows just how dangerous he has become. Well, almost nobody.

Fortunately, the scene is up on YouTube in case you haven't seen it or it escapes your memory. It's really a well-done sequence that communicates so much visually. Dafoe barely has to say anything for the tension to build, and watching Norman slowly put the pieces together is almost as uncomfortable as it is entertaining. Raimi also deserves credit for letting the awkward silences do some of the heavy lifting. You can practically feel Peter's uneasiness growing as the dinner goes on. It's too bad the Thanksgiving dinner had to end before Osborn cut the turkey.

The real tension comes when Norman notices Peter's injuries. He's already suspicious, and the conversation gives him another reason to wonder whether the young photographer has something to hide. Then he makes the connection. Peter is Spider-Man . The realization changes everything about their relationship, even though Peter doesn't know Norman has figured it out. That's what makes the scene so effective. There's no dramatic villain reveal or elaborate explanation. Norman simply sits there and quietly works out the truth. Dafoe barely needs to raise his voice. His expression does most of the work, and suddenly that Thanksgiving turkey doesn't look quite so appetizing.

One of the things I enjoyed about Raimi's Spider-Man is how much attention it gives Peter's maturing life outside the costume. The movie understands that being a superhero is only part of his problem. He's struggling financially, trying to impress Mary Jane, and worrying about Aunt May. He also has to deal with Harry's increasingly complicated relationship with his father. That's a lot for one teenager to manage, even before somebody starts throwing pumpkins at him. The Thanksgiving scene brings all those relationships into one room. Peter wants a normal evening with the people he cares about, but Norman's presence makes that practically impossible.

That's what makes Norman such a great villain. He doesn't need to blow up a building or send another pumpkin bomb flying through New York to make Peter's life miserable. He's already sitting at the same dinner table as the people Peter loves. He knows Harry, he knows Aunt May, and now he knows Peter's secret. That's a pretty awful combination for a teenager who already has enough trouble keeping his personal life together. Dafoe plays the whole thing beautifully, too. There's something genuinely unsettling about watching him smile through dinner while knowing what he's figured out. I've always loved how Raimi lets that moment breathe instead of rushing off to the next big action sequence. The Green Goblin has plenty of spectacular entrances, but his most frightening appearance might just be the one where he's holding a fork.
